title: Chapter IV
paragraphs: What foolish weathercocks we are! I had resolved to keep myself free of all human company and thanked my lucky stars for finding a place where company was almost impossible. Yet I, weak creature, after struggling with loneliness and low spirits until dusk, finally had to surrender. Pretending I needed information about running the household, I asked Mrs. Dean to sit with me when she brought my supper. I sincerely hoped she would turn out to be an inveterate gossip, whose talk would either restore my spirits or send me to sleep.
“You’ve lived here a long time,” I began. “Didn’t you say sixteen years?”
“Eighteen, sir. I came to look after the mistress when she married; after her death, the master kept me on as his housekeeper.”
“Really.”

A silence followed. I feared she was no gossip, unless it concerned her own affairs, which could hardly interest me. But after sitting in thought for a while, a fist on each knee and a thoughtful cloud over her rosy face, she exclaimed, “Ah, things have changed a great deal since then!”
“Yes,” I observed, “I suppose you’ve witnessed quite a few changes?”
“I have, and troubles along with them,” she replied.

“Ah, I’ll bring up my landlord’s family!” I thought. “A promising subject to begin with! And I’d like to hear about that pretty young widow: whether she was born here, or, more probably, is a foreign growth that the surly _indigenae_—the natives—refuse to recognise as one of their own.” With that purpose, I asked Mrs. Dean why Heathcliff rented out Thrushcross Grange and chose to live in a house and location so much beneath it. “Does he lack the money to keep this estate in good order?” I asked.

“Money, sir!” she answered. “Nobody knows how much he has, and there’s more every year. Yes, yes, he can afford a grander house than this, but he’s very tight—close-fisted. Even if he’d intended to move to Thrushcross Grange, once he heard of a good tenant he couldn’t have passed up the chance of a few hundred pounds more. It’s strange how greedy people can be when they’ve nobody else in the world!”
“Apparently he had a son?”
“Yes, he had one son—now he’s dead.”
“And the young woman, Mrs. Heathcliff, is that son’s widow?”
“Yes.”
“Where was she from in the first place?”

“Why, sir, she’s my late master’s daughter. Before her marriage she was Catherine Linton. I was her nurse, poor thing! I did hope Mr. Heathcliff would move here; then she and I might have been together again.”

“What! Catherine Linton?” I exclaimed in astonishment. A moment’s thought, though, persuaded me that this was not my ghostly Catherine. “Then,” I went on, “the previous occupant here was called Linton?”
“Yes, he was.”
“And who is Earnshaw—Hareton Earnshaw, the young man living with Mr. Heathcliff? Are the two related?”
“No. He’s the late Mrs. Linton’s nephew.”
“So he’s the young woman’s cousin?”
“Yes, and her husband was her cousin too: one on her mother’s side, the other on her father’s. Heathcliff married Mr. Linton’s sister.”
“I noticed ‘Earnshaw’ carved above the front door at Wuthering Heights. Is the family an old one?”
“Very old, sir; and Hareton is the last of them, just as our Miss Cathy is the last of us—I mean the Lintons. Have you visited Wuthering Heights? Forgive my asking, but I’d like to know how she is!”
“Mrs. Heathcliff? She looked quite healthy and very lovely, though I think she wasn’t especially happy.”
“Oh dear, that doesn’t surprise me! And what did you think of the master?”
“A rather rough sort, Mrs. Dean. Isn’t that what people say of him?”
“Rough as a saw and hard as whinstone rock! The less you have to do with him, the better.”
“Life must have given him some ups and downs to make him so disagreeable. Do you know his story?”

“It’s the story of a cuckoo, sir. I know all of it, except where he was born, who his parents were, and how he first got his money. And Hareton’s been pushed out like a dunnock fledgling before it can fly! That unlucky lad is the only person in this parish who doesn’t suspect how he’s been cheated.”
“Well, Mrs. Dean, telling me about my neighbours would be an act of kindness. I don’t think I could sleep if I went to bed, so please sit and talk for an hour.”
“Of course, sir! I’ll get some sewing, then sit for as long as you like. But you’ve caught a cold: I saw you shaking, and you must have some gruel to drive it away.”

The good woman bustled out, and I huddled closer to the fire. My head was hot and the rest of me cold; besides, my nerves and brain were excited almost to the point of absurdity. This did not make me uncomfortable so much as afraid—as I still am—that today’s and yesterday’s adventures might have serious consequences. Soon she returned with a steaming bowl and a sewing basket. She put the bowl on the hearth and drew her chair closer, evidently pleased to find me so ready for company.

Before I came here, she began, without waiting for another invitation to tell her story, I was nearly always at Wuthering Heights. My mother had nursed Mr. Hindley Earnshaw—Hareton’s father—and I grew used to playing with the children. I ran errands too, helped with the haymaking, and stayed about the farm ready to do whatever anyone found for me. One fine summer morning, at the start of harvest, I remember, old Mr. Earnshaw came downstairs dressed for a journey. After telling Joseph what work needed doing that day, he turned to Hindley, Cathy and me, for I was eating porridge with them, and said to his son, “Now, my bonny lad, I’m going to Liverpool today. What shall I bring you? Choose what you like, only keep it small, because I’m walking there and back: sixty miles each way, and that’s a long stretch!” Hindley asked for a fiddle. Then he asked Miss Cathy, who was barely six but could ride any horse in the stable; she chose a whip. He remembered me too: his heart was kind, though sometimes he was rather strict. He promised me a pocketful of apples and pears, then kissed his children, said goodbye and set off.

Those three days he was away seemed a long time to all of us, and little Cathy often asked when he would come home. Mrs. Earnshaw expected him by supper on the third evening and delayed the meal hour after hour. Still there was no sign of him, and at last the children tired of running to the gate to look. Darkness fell. She wanted them in bed, but they pleaded so sadly to stay up that she let them. At about eleven the latch lifted quietly and the master stepped inside. He dropped into a chair, laughing and groaning, and told everyone to stand back: he was nearly dead, and wouldn’t make another walk like that for the three kingdoms.

“And to be scolded to death at the end of it!” he said, unfolding the greatcoat bundled in his arms. “Look here, wife! Nothing in my life has worn me out like this. But you must take it as a gift from God, though it’s almost as dark as if it came from the devil.”

We crowded around. Over Miss Cathy’s head I glimpsed a dirty, ragged child with black hair, big enough to walk and talk—its face actually looked older than Catherine’s. Yet when it was put on its feet it only stared round and kept repeating some gibberish nobody could understand. I was frightened; Mrs. Earnshaw was ready to throw it outside. She flew into a rage, asking how he could bring that gypsy brat into the house when they had their own children to feed and provide for. What did he intend to do with it? Was he mad? The master tried to explain, but he really was half dead with exhaustion. Through her scolding I could make out only that he had seen it starving and homeless, and practically unable to speak, in the streets of Liverpool. He had picked it up and asked who it belonged to. Nobody knew, he said; and as he had little time or money to spare, he thought it better to bring it straight home than incur useless expenses there, since he was determined not to abandon it as he had found it. Well, in the end my mistress grumbled herself quiet, and Mr. Earnshaw told me to wash it, find clean clothes for it and let it sleep with the children.

Hindley and Cathy were content to watch and listen until peace returned. Then they both searched their father’s pockets for the promised presents. Hindley was fourteen, but when he pulled out what remained of a fiddle, crushed to pieces inside the greatcoat, he burst into noisy tears. Cathy, discovering that the master had lost her whip while caring for the stranger, showed her temper by baring her teeth and spitting at the uncomprehending little thing. For this she earned a hard blow from her father, to teach her better manners. They absolutely refused to let it share their bed, or even their room. I had no more sense than they did, so I left it on the stair landing, hoping it might be gone by morning. By chance, or perhaps drawn by the sound of his voice, it crept to Mr. Earnshaw’s door, where he found it when he came out. He asked how it got there. I had to confess, and was sent away from the house as punishment for my cowardice and cruelty.

That was how Heathcliff first entered the family. When I came back a few days later—for I did not consider my banishment permanent—I found they had named him “Heathcliff,” after a son who had died in childhood. Ever since, it has served him as both first name and surname. He and Miss Cathy were now close friends, but Hindley hated him, and, truthfully, so did I. We tormented and persecuted him shamefully: I lacked the sense to recognise my unfairness, and our mistress never said a word for him when she saw him mistreated.

He seemed a sullen, enduring child, perhaps already hardened to abuse. He took Hindley’s blows without a flinch or a tear, and when I pinched him he only drew a breath and opened his eyes, as though he had hurt himself accidentally and nobody was responsible. Such endurance enraged old Earnshaw whenever he caught his son tormenting what he called the poor fatherless child. He grew strangely fond of Heathcliff and believed everything he said—though to be fair, the boy said very little, and usually told the truth. He indulged him much more than Cathy, who was too mischievous and wilful to be a favourite.

So he created ill feeling in the house from the start. By the time Mrs. Earnshaw died, less than two years later, the young master had come to see his father as a tyrant rather than a friend, and Heathcliff as someone who had stolen his father’s affection and his own privileges. Brooding over these wrongs made him bitter. For a while I sympathised, but I changed my mind when the children caught measles and I had to nurse them, taking on a grown woman’s responsibilities all at once. Heathcliff was dangerously ill and, at his worst, wanted me constantly beside his pillow. I suppose he realised how much I did for him and did not have the sense to see I was obliged to do it. But I will say this: no nurse ever looked after a quieter child. The contrast with the others forced me to be fairer. Cathy and her brother pestered me dreadfully; _he_ was as uncomplaining as a lamb, though it was hardness rather than gentleness that made him so little trouble.

He recovered, and the doctor said it was largely thanks to me, praising my care. His praise made me vain and softened me towards the creature through whom I had earned it, so Hindley lost his last supporter. Still, I could not be devoted to Heathcliff, and often wondered what my master found so admirable in that sullen boy, who, as far as I remember, never repaid his kindness with any sign of gratitude. He was not rude to his benefactor, simply unfeeling, although he knew perfectly well how strongly he held his affection and that he need only speak for the whole household to bow to his wishes. For example, I remember Mr. Earnshaw buying two young horses at the parish fair and giving one to each boy. Heathcliff chose the better-looking one, but it soon went lame. When he discovered this, he told Hindley—

“You’ll have to swap horses with me. I don’t like mine; and if you won’t, I’ll tell your father about the three beatings you’ve given me this week and show him my arm: it’s black all the way to the shoulder.” Hindley stuck his tongue out and struck him about the ears. “You’d better do it now,” he insisted, retreating to the doorway—they were in the stable. “You’ll have to; and if I mention these blows, you’ll get them back with interest.” “Get out, dog!” Hindley shouted, threatening him with an iron weight used for weighing hay and potatoes. “Throw it,” he answered, standing his ground, “and I’ll tell him how you boasted you’d throw me out as soon as he died. See if he doesn’t throw you out at once.” Hindley hurled it, striking him in the chest. He fell, but immediately struggled upright, pale and breathless. If I had not stopped him, he would have gone straight to the master and taken full revenge by letting his condition speak for him and indicating who had caused it. “Take my colt then, Gypsy!” young Earnshaw said. “And I pray he breaks your neck. Take him and be damned, you beggarly intruder! Coax my father out of everything he’s got; only show him afterwards what you are, you little devil.—And take that! I hope the horse kicks your brains out!”

Heathcliff had gone to untie the horse and move it into his own stall. As he passed behind it, Hindley ended his speech by knocking him beneath its feet, then ran away as fast as he could without waiting to see whether his wishes came true. I was surprised how calmly the child picked himself up and went on with his plan, exchanging the saddles and everything else. Afterwards he sat on a bundle of hay until the sickness caused by the heavy blow passed, before going into the house. I easily persuaded him to let me blame the horse for his bruises: he cared little what story was told, now he had what he wanted. Indeed, he complained so rarely about disturbances like these that I really believed he was not revengeful. As you will hear, I was completely mistaken.
